summary:
Lunar and Martian Outpost Game is a browser-based web game, and Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is the challenge or the objective of the web game that I have built with Django for ages 7–12. I developed an interactive space-habitat simulator that uses real NASA DONKI space weather APIs and planetary radiation datasets to teach young learners how astronauts survive on the Moon and Mars.

It addresses the challenge of making complex aerospace engineering and space-weather physics accessible without oversimplifying the science. Players manage a strict power budget across Air, Greenhouse, Storm Shield, Science, and Radio systems—forcing real-time strategic trade-offs against unwarned solar flares, multi-day Martian dust storms, communication delays, and the 14-day lunar night. Powered by a pure-Python simulation engine and file-based Django sessions with zero database setup, the app runs seamlessly in any browser.

This project is important because it transforms passive STEM learning into active, data-driven problem-solving, inspiring the next generation of explorers to understand the real environmental hazards of deep-space habitation.

Architecturally, the pure-Python simulation logic resides independently in game/engine.py, making it easily testable without Django dependencies. NASA data fetching and static archives are handled in game/nasa.py and game/data.py, while game/views.py, alongside accompanying templates and static files, drives the web-based user interface.
details:
LMOS-LUNAR and MARTIAN SIMULATOR

WHAT IT DOES

Our project, "Lunar and Martian Outpost Simulator," is an interactive educational tool designed to introduce children (ages 7-12) to the concepts of space outposts and the challenges of radiation in extraterrestrial environments. The application simulates the conditions on the Moon and Mars, allowing users to build virtual habitats, experiment with protective materials, and observe the impact of radiation on their outpost design choices. The simulator integrates real NASA datasets for environmental conditions and radiation levels, providing an authentic learning experience.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

The primary benefit is making complex scientific concepts accessible and engaging for young students. By visualizing and interacting with outpost design and radiation protection strategies, children gain a foundational understanding of space science and engineering. This can inspire future interest in STEM fields and foster critical thinking and problem-solving skills from an early age.

We aim to bridge the knowledge gap for children unfamiliar with space science, particularly regarding outposts and radiation. By gamifying the learning experience, the project encourages curiosity and demystifies space missions, supporting educational outreach efforts aligned with NASA’s mission.

  • Programming Language: Django, HTML (HyperText Markup Language), CSS (Cascading Style Sheets), JavaScript.
  • Data Sources: NASA Open Data resources (environmental and radiation data for Moon and Mars)

Our simulator stands out by blending interactive gameplay with real scientific data, offering a hands-on approach to understanding space outposts. The visual representation of radiation shielding, the ability to test different materials, and instant feedback on design choices make the learning process dynamic and memorable. The project is tailored for children, using age-appropriate language, appealing visuals, and a user-friendly interface.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific accuracy, validated against JPL Horizons
  • Only real NASA data, with no fake values
  • Works on any device: desktop and phone
  • A clean interface that non-experts can understand
  • Open-source code anyone can inspect and build on


We focused on accessibility, ensuring the simulator runs on standard computers without additional hardware. The interface was designed to be intuitive for young users. We also prioritized scientific accuracy by using real NASA datasets and incorporated feedback mechanisms to continually improve educational effectiveness. Additionally, we ensured that all code and assets are open-source and properly credited, in line with Space Apps Challenge requirements.
